title: Aristotle
summary: Aristotle was an ancient Greek philosopher, a student of Plato and teacher of Alexander the Great, and the founder of a school at the Lyceum in Athens. He investigated almost everything, from animals to politics. In ethics his central question is what a good, full life is — "eudaimonia" — and how to reach it through virtue, understood as a "mean" between extremes, through friendship and through reasoned choice.
onEmotions: Aristotle was the first to analyze the emotions systematically: in the second book of the Rhetoric he describes anger, fear, shame, pity, envy, indignation and other feelings — what causes them, whom they are directed at and how they subside. For him feelings are not enemies of reason: they are accompanied by pain or pleasure and depend on how we understand what is happening. Feelings in themselves are neither good nor bad — we are judged by our settled character. Virtue is a "mean": to feel an emotion at the right time, toward the right person, and to the right degree. And tragedy, according to the Poetics, brings about "catharsis" — a purification of the emotions — through pity and fear.

anxiety.text: Aristotle taught while strolling the walkways of the Lyceum — hence his school's name, the Peripatetics, "the walkers." If anxiety is wearing you down, he has an observation that helps a great deal. In On the Soul he notes that sometimes people feel everything a frightened person feels even though nothing frightening is happening: the body can be tuned to fear before any reason appears. Every feeling, for Aristotle, is at once a bodily movement and a thought about what is going on. In the Rhetoric he adds that fear arises from imagining a misfortune that seems near, while distant things hardly frighten us. Anxiety is often exactly this: the imagination pulling the future closer. Aristotle also reminds us that deliberating — "taking counsel with ourselves" — makes sense only about things that depend on us. Separating those from everything else is already half the relief.
anxiety.practice: Take a five-minute peripatetic walk: go slowly, and as you walk, sort what worries you into "up to me" and "not up to me." When you get back, choose one small step from the first pile.

fear.text: Aristotle likened virtue to archery: missing is easy, hitting the mark is hard. He never thought fear shameful — the only question is where it aims. Courage, for him, is not fearlessness but a "mean" between two extremes: cowardice, when fear governs everything, and rashness, when a person fails to see real danger. Someone who fears absolutely nothing, Aristotle said, is closer to insensible or mad than brave. The courageous person fears what ought to be feared, in the way it ought to be feared, and still does what they believe is right. In the Rhetoric fear is defined as pain and disturbance arising from the thought of an impending evil. So fear has an object, and it can be examined: how real is the danger, how near is it, and what is in your power? Your fear is not a verdict but a signal you can talk with.
fear.practice: Picture a target: cowardice on the left, rashness on the right, courage in the center. Say aloud where your fear is right now, and one small action that would move it a finger's width closer to the center.

sadness.text: "One swallow does not make a spring," wrote Aristotle, nor one day a happy life. Nor does one sad day make an unhappy one — and he never demanded constant cheerfulness. In his Rhetoric almost every emotion is described as accompanied by pain or pleasure: sadness is a natural part of how we respond to the world. In the Ethics he notes that pain is driven out by pleasure — its opposite or any strong one. He also asks whether the presence of friends lightens grief: do they share the weight with us, or does the very joy of their company soften the pain? He doesn't settle on an answer, but he has no doubt that friends help. Sadness doesn't have to be conquered by effort. You can let it be, and beside it leave room for something alive: a person, a task, a simple pleasure.
sadness.practice: Today, do one small thing that usually brings you quiet pleasure — not instead of the sadness but alongside it. Aristotle would say a lively pleasure will make room for itself on its own.

grief.text: Thinking about happiness, Aristotle recalled old Priam, who lost his sons and his Troy, and admitted honestly that such misfortunes cloud even the most worthy life. Reason, he held, does not cancel grief — good and bad fortune really do matter. But he added that nobility shines through even in misfortune, when a person bears the weight not out of insensitivity but out of greatness of soul. And about friends: in grief their presence eases the pain, as if they take part of the burden on themselves. Aristotle noticed that strong people are reluctant to burden those close to them with their pain. But grief shared is lighter. It is the very friendship he considered necessary for life.
grief.practice: Spend some time today near someone close — over tea or simply in silence, without even talking about the loss. Aristotle believed a friend's presence alone takes on part of the weight.

loneliness.text: "Whoever can live outside a community is either a beast or a god," wrote Aristotle. A human being is neither, and that is why loneliness hurts so much: it touches our deepest need. In the Politics he calls the human being by nature a creature that lives in community — a "political" animal. In the Nicomachean Ethics he asks whether a happy person who has everything needs friends, and answers yes: no one would choose to have all good things on their own. Through a friend, "another self," we even feel our own life more fully. So your longing for people is the voice of human nature. And Aristotle hints that friendship grows from small things: goodwill, a shared task, time spent together.
loneliness.practice: Think of one person toward whom you feel even a little goodwill — for Aristotle, every friendship begins there. Take a step toward them: a short message, a question, an invitation.

quote.text: Man is by nature a political animal.
quote.author: Aristotle

anger.text: "Anyone can become angry — that is easy," wrote Aristotle; the hard part is being angry with the right person, in the right way. He didn't ask you to be ashamed of anger — here he is surprisingly on your side. In the Rhetoric he gave the first detailed analysis of anger: pain plus a desire to answer a "slight," to being not taken seriously. And in the Nicomachean Ethics he writes that someone who doesn't get angry when they should seems a fool and ready to put up with insults — that, too, is a defect. Virtue, for Aristotle, is not the absence of anger but a "mean." So the useful question isn't "how do I stop being angry" but "what here was actually unjust, and what measure of response would be right?" Your anger may be pointing to something important.
anger.practice: Write one sentence: "What hurt me was that…" — and measure your response the Aristotelian way: no more and no less than the situation deserves. What would that response be?

quote.text: Anyone can get angry — that is easy… but to do this to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive, and in the right way, that is not for everyone, nor is it easy.
quote.author: Aristotle

shame.text: Aristotle noticed that shame shows on the outside: we blush from it as we pale from fear — a feeling, not a trait. When ashamed, you want to hide, and it is agonizing. In the Rhetoric he describes shame as pain and disturbance about things that may damage our good name, and notes that we feel shame above all before those whose opinion we value. In the Ethics he says shame suits the young: while still learning to live we make mistakes, and shame holds us back from worse. Another distinction of his matters too: it only really makes sense to be ashamed of what depends on us — our actions, not what has happened to us. So shame is a sign that you care. You can listen to it, take a lesson from it, and not let it pass judgment on the whole of you.
shame.practice: Ask yourself Aristotle's question aloud: "Am I ashamed of something I did, or of something that happened to me?" If it was something you did, name one thing you'll do differently; if it happened to you, let it go at least for today.

guilt.text: Aristotle has a captain who throws the cargo overboard in a storm to save the ship: a choice was made, but no one would make it in calm weather. Guilt is heavy, but it shows that justice matters to you. Aristotle distinguished voluntary and involuntary acts: something done out of ignorance or under the pressure of circumstances, which the person later regrets, he did not regard as malice. He called such acts "mixed." And about justice he wrote that its essence is to restore an equality that has been broken — not to punish yourself, but to set things right as far as possible. Guilt is not a reason for endless self-reproach but a question: what exactly can I restore or make good now?
guilt.practice: Choose one action that, in Aristotle's sense, restores a broken equality: give something back, apologize, help. Do it today or set a time for it.

envy.text: An old proverb Aristotle quotes: "potter envies potter" — we envy not the king but our equals and neighbors. In the Rhetoric he analyzed this hard-to-admit feeling with remarkable precision: pain at another's good fortune. Right alongside it he described its "relative," emulation, in Greek "zelos": pain that another has a good we lack but could also attain. The difference is in direction: envy wants the other to have less, emulation wants me to have more. Aristotle considered the second a feeling of decent people; it moves us to grow. Your envy is raw material. You can recast it by asking: what exactly do I want for myself?
envy.practice: Write: "I envy that he/she has…" — then recast the envy into zelos: "I want for myself…" Name one step in that direction.

emptiness.text: The first line of the Nicomachean Ethics: every art and every action seems to aim at some good. When nothing seems to matter, it is a hard state, and it is not your fault. Aristotle began his ethics with a question very close to yours: what is it all for? And there must be an end we choose for its own sake. He called it "eudaimonia" — not a passing pleasure but the fullness of life, flourishing. And he believed it consists in activity: the flute player has their work, the carpenter theirs, and a human being's work is to live, acting and understanding meaningfully. Emptiness may mean that right now your life holds little activity of your own — things you do for their own sake. You don't have to find it all at once. You can start with something small that genuinely interests you.
emptiness.practice: Recall an activity in which you once lost track of time — Aristotle would call it activity for its own sake. Give it ten minutes today without thinking about the result.

confusion.text: "All human beings by nature desire to know" — so begins Aristotle's Metaphysics, and knowing, he thought, begins with perplexity. Feeling lost is unpleasant, but for Aristotle it is where any understanding begins. He called this state by the Greek word "aporia" — literally "no way through," an impasse. In the Metaphysics he writes that anyone who wants to get to the bottom of things must first be properly puzzled: someone who hasn't gone through perplexity is like a traveler who doesn't know where to go. And in the Nicomachean Ethics he advises us not to demand more precision from a subject than it allows: in matters of life, clarity comes "in outline," not as in mathematics. So your confusion is not a failure but an honest sign that the question is hard. You can explore it calmly, naming exactly what is unclear.
confusion.practice: Tell someone about your "aporia" — aloud, as two or three concrete questions. Aristotle reasoned with his students as they walked: a precisely posed question is often already half the answer.

quote.text: All men by nature desire to know.
quote.author: Aristotle

fatigue.text: The Greek word schole, leisure, gave us the word "school": for Aristotle free time was not emptiness but the highest value. Tiredness is not a sign of laziness but the honest voice of a living being. Aristotle soberly observed that nothing human is capable of continuous activity; that's why even pleasure in the same thing fades over time. He considered rest necessary: we need it because we cannot work without a break. He agreed with the sage Anacharsis, who advised playing so as to be able to do serious work afterward. Rest, for Aristotle, exists for the sake of activity, not the other way round. Tiredness is no reason to reproach yourself but a sign that it's time to give yourself a breather.
fatigue.practice: Give yourself a quarter of an hour of schole — real leisure with no tasks and no screens: sit, look out the window, produce nothing. And don't justify it, even to yourself.

boredom.text: Aristotle had no separate teaching on boredom, but he noticed why new things delight us more: at first the mind is focused and alert, then attention slackens — and the pleasure dims. He would recognize the dragging, grey state you are in. Boredom, then, is not the emptiness of the world but the tiredness of attention. For Aristotle, pleasure is not a separate thing but what accompanies an activity and completes it when it is carried out at full strength. So the way out of boredom is not a search for ever stronger sensations but a real return to some activity, with your attention switched on.
boredom.practice: Pick something ordinary — tea, a walk, washing a cup — and do it "at full strength," as Aristotle would say: with full attention to the details, as if for the first time.

joy.text: "Pleasure completes an activity as the bloom of youth completes the young," wrote Aristotle, arguing with those who found joy suspicious. It isn't glued onto life from outside but blossoms from within when we do something at full strength and without hindrance. He would have taken your joy seriously. The best joys, for Aristotle, are those bound up with good activity: understanding, friendship, work that goes well for us. And eudaimonia — happiness as the fullness of life — is unthinkable without pleasure. So your joy is not a chance gift to be hidden away quickly but a sign that life is going well right now. You can simply live it to the full.
joy.practice: Say aloud, like a formula: "I feel good when I…" — and finish it with the activity your joy blossomed from. Aristotle thought it worth knowing by sight.

love.text: Asked what a friend is, Aristotle is said to have answered: "A single soul dwelling in two bodies." He counted love among life's greatest goods and devoted two books of the Nicomachean Ethics to philia. He spoke of "philia" — a word that covers friendship, love and family affection alike. He distinguished three kinds: for the sake of usefulness, for the sake of pleasure, and for the sake of the person themselves, their character. The last is the most lasting: in it we wish the other good for their own sake. The beloved, for Aristotle, becomes "another self": we feel their joys and sorrows almost as our own. He also observed that love consists more in loving than in being loved. Your feeling is one of the peaks of human life, not something to be kept under control.
love.practice: Tell this person today one thing you value in them for their own sake — not for what they give you. Aristotle would call this friendship for the person's own sake.

gratitude.text: Aristotle noticed something curious: a benefactor usually loves the one they helped more than they are loved in return — as a craftsman loves his work. The warm gratitude you feel now is the answering thread of that same bond. In the Rhetoric he examined "charis" — kindness, a readiness to help not for one's own benefit but for the sake of the one being helped. Gratitude is the response to such selfless help. In the Nicomachean Ethics he notes that some people — parents, teachers — can never be repaid in equal measure, and there is nothing shameful in that: we can repay with what is in our power. Gratitude is also the recognition of a bond in which you matter too. You are not a debtor; you are a participant in a shared good.
gratitude.practice: Respond today to one person you are grateful to — with a word, attention, a little help, as far as you are able. Not everyone can be repaid in equal measure, Aristotle says, but repaying what you can is already just.

hope.text: An acorn, for Aristotle, is an oak "in potentiality": it already holds what it is able to become. Your hope is the same way of seeing your life — as something not yet finished. In the Rhetoric he writes that the young live by hope, because hope looks to the future and they have a great deal of future ahead; this makes them bolder and quicker to take heart. Aristotle has a fitting concept: "potentiality," in Greek "dynamis" — what has not yet become actual but is able to. Hope keeps that possibility open. At the same time Aristotle advised practical wisdom: it helps to see which steps toward what you want really depend on you. Then hope becomes not waiting but the beginning of action.
hope.practice: Note your hope, and next to it one action within your power that moves the possible a little toward the actual: the acorn one step closer to the oak.

nostalgia.text: "Sweet it is to remember toils once past," Aristotle quotes Euripides in the Rhetoric. The bittersweet feeling you have now was something he understood well. In the Rhetoric he observed that older people live more by memory than by hope, because they have more past than future — and that remembering can be pleasant in itself. That is, even hard times can become dear in memory — because we lived through them and endured. Nostalgia is not an escape from the present but a way of sensing the wholeness of your life. Eudaimonia, for Aristotle, is the fullness of a whole life, not of a single day, and the past is part of it. You can allow yourself to remember with gratitude.
nostalgia.practice: Tell someone a story from the time you miss — with details, the way one tells of toils once past. Notice what from that life still lives in you now.

craving.text: Aristotle compared desire to a child who needs a kind tutor: the child isn't punished for wanting but taught to listen. The sharp "I want it now" is part of our nature, and there is nothing to be ashamed of. He called this kind of desire "epithymia" — an appetite for the pleasant that lives in the non-rational part of the soul. He didn't urge us to root it out: desire is not to be crushed but taught to listen to reason. He also honestly noted that a desire that is constantly indulged grows and can drown out reasoning. And he described "weakness of will" — when a person knows what is better, but passion clouds that knowledge for a while, as in someone asleep or drunk. It helps to remember that this wave rises and passes, while your knowledge of what you really want stays with you.
craving.practice: When the craving rolls in, set a timer for ten minutes and spend them like a tutor with a child: walk around, drink some water, breathe. The wave will rise and fall — notice the moment it starts to ebb.

addiction.text: Aristotle compared the weak-willed person to a city that has good laws but doesn't use them. In this picture addiction is not a moral failure and not a verdict on your character. Aristotle examined in detail a state he called "akrasia" — weakness of will: a person knows what is better for them, but at the decisive moment passion wins. Importantly, Aristotle distinguished such a person from a vicious one: the weak-willed person regrets what they have done, which means their values are alive and they are capable of change. Aristotle also knew the power of habit — he said that habit becomes a kind of second nature, yet it is easier to change than nature. The path, in his view, is not a burst of willpower but the gradual forming of new habits, step by step.
addiction.practice: Name aloud three of your "good laws" — what you value most in life. And if you'd like support in living by them again, you can talk with people who know this path, for example in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: Aristotle advised straightening yourself the way you straighten a bent stick — little by little, bending it the other way. The heavy morning after, that mix of bodily weakness and regret, is a state he would recognize. He wrote that a weak-willed person, unlike a vicious one, regrets what they did afterward. That sounds bitter, but it is good news: regret means you don't agree with what happened, and your values are in place. The "mean," in his view, is found by moving away from the extreme you are more drawn to. At the same time he was a realist: we reach the mean not in a day but through repetition. Today is not the time to put yourself on trial. Today is the time to look after your body and think calmly.
hangover.practice: Look after your body first: water, fresh air, quiet. Then tell yourself in one sentence, without reproach, what you'd like to do differently next time — the first gentle bend of the stick.

euphoria.text: "God always enjoys a single and simple pleasure," wrote Aristotle, while we, complicated creatures, need change. A high, when everything seems bright and possible, is a wonderful feeling, and there's no need to spoil it. In the Nicomachean Ethics Aristotle explained why change is so sweet: our nature is not simple, there is a lot in us, and we are glad when something changes. Your euphoria is a full-fledged human experience, a surge of life. Aristotle did add that the most reliable joys are those born of activity: of work, understanding, friendship. So you can simply enjoy the high, and at the same time notice what exactly has come so alive in you right now. That will be useful later, too, when the wave recedes.
euphoria.practice: Write down what you are feeling now, what seems possible, and what exactly has come so alive in you. Reread it on an ordinary day, like a letter from yourself.

crash.text: Aristotle's Poetics calls a sudden reversal of fortune "peripeteia." After a high, the drop can be very hard: the world seems gray, the recent brightness a trick. For him happiness, eudaimonia, is not the state of a single day but a quality of a whole life taken together. Just as one warm day doesn't make a summer, one hard day doesn't make a life a failure. He also explained that our nature is not simple, and so change is inevitable in it: a high is followed by a low, strain by fatigue. That doesn't mean the joy was false, nor that the grayness is the truth about the world. It is a wave. Aristotle believed that support comes not from peaks but from steady things: a familiar routine, work, friends. You can lean on them until the wave passes.
crash.practice: Choose one simple, familiar thing for today — a walk, a meal at the usual time, a call to a friend — and do it, demanding nothing more of yourself. Aristotle would look for support in such steady things, not in peaks.

quote.text: For one swallow does not make a summer, nor does one day.
quote.author: Aristotle

panic.text: For Aristotle every feeling is both a movement of the body and a thought: anger, he wrote, is at once "a boiling of the blood around the heart" and a desire to answer an injury. When panic hits, it is very frightening: it feels as if your body has slipped out of control. Aristotle was not a psychologist in today's sense, but in On the Soul he made an important observation: sometimes a person feels everything a frightened person feels, even though there is nothing frightening around. So a wave of terror can begin in the body and only afterward find thoughts to go with it. It helps to return to the body without arguing with the thoughts. Such a wave usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and feel the support. Breathe out slowly and go through the five senses Aristotle examined in On the Soul: name aloud one thing you see, hear, touch, smell and taste.

dread.text: Aristotle advised deliberating only about what is possible and up to us — no one deliberates about the stars or the past. A heavy foreboding, when something dark seems to lie ahead but it's unclear what, is one of the most exhausting states. In the Rhetoric Aristotle defined fear as pain at the thought of a misfortune that seems near. The weight of foreboding likely grows when fear has no clear object: the imagination makes the misfortune both near and elusive. "Taking counsel with oneself" means calmly considering what is possible, what is likely and what depends on us. And he reminded us that courage is not the absence of fear but the readiness to remain yourself alongside it. You don't have to get rid of the foreboding right away. Step by step you can give it back its outlines and separate the vague from the real.
dread.practice: Take counsel with yourself the Aristotelian way, aloud: "What is possible? What is likely? What depends on me?" One short sentence for each. At the end, name one thing that is all right just now.

fomo.text: Aristotle opened his Ethics with an argument about where to look for happiness: some find it in pleasure, some in honors, some in wealth. The feeling that real life is happening somewhere else, to other people, is a similar trap. Many, he writes, see the good in honors, but honors are too superficial to be a real goal: they depend more on those who confer them than on the one who receives them. Happiness, on the other hand, should be something of our own, hard to take away. And further: eudaimonia is the fullness of a whole life, not a collection of bright events. No one can be everywhere and take part in everything — life is made of choices, not of being present everywhere. Aristotle would suggest asking: is what I'm afraid of missing my own good, or just someone else's glitter?
fomo.practice: Imagine yourself a year from now looking back at this evening: what of the things you are "missing" will you remember — and what of what you are doing right now? Aristotle measured happiness by a whole life, not a single event.

sleepless.text: Aristotle wrote a short treatise On Sleep and Waking — and in it sleep looks not like a feat but like a gift of nature. When the night passes without sleep and thoughts in the dark seem heavier than by day, it wears you out. He held that living beings need sleep because none of them can be active all the time: sleep is a natural rest that exists for the sake of waking. Sleep is not a task to be accomplished by effort but something nature brings on its own when it isn't interfered with. Trying to force yourself to sleep often only keeps the mind tense. Night thoughts, too, are worth taking with caution: in On Dreams Aristotle shows that when outside impressions quiet down, the images of the imagination become especially vivid and easily seem like reality to us.
sleepless.practice: Instead of trying to fall asleep, simply rest lying down, as Aristotle — for whom sleep comes on its own — would advise: feel the weight of your body and exhale slowly. Tell a persistent thought: "We'll deliberate in the morning."

betrayal.text: Aristotle held that deceiving someone by feigning love is worse than counterfeiting coin: something far more valuable has been forged. Betrayal wounds deeply — the blow comes from someone you trusted. Aristotle thought a lot about how friendships fall apart. He distinguished friendship for usefulness, for pleasure and for the person themselves, and noted that it is especially painful when we thought we were loved for our own sake and it turned out to be for gain. This is an important confirmation: your pain is proportionate to what was damaged. But Aristotle offers comfort too: being deceived doesn't mean you were foolish. Trust is part of friendship; without it friendship is impossible. The other person betrayed, and your capacity to love is still with you.
betrayal.practice: Write down what you valued in this relationship — it speaks of your values, not your naivety. Then name one person you can still trust.

jealousy.text: Aristotle observed that being in love is a kind of excess of friendship, and so it turns toward one person: you can't be in love with many at once. He didn't write about jealousy separately, but much follows from this thought. The agonizing mix of fear of losing someone you love, hurt and pain is tied to the very nature of such love — its exclusiveness. In the Rhetoric he writes that we are especially stung by slights from those close to us, from whom we expect good. Jealousy may be a signal of fear of such a slight. It's worth listening to — not as an order to act, but as a question: what am I missing in our relationship right now?
jealousy.practice: Say two sentences to yourself: "I'm afraid that…" and "I wish that…" The second can be said calmly to the person you love: it speaks not of suspicion but of what you are missing.

resentment.text: Aristotle had a sharp word — "sulky," literally "bitter": people who keep their anger inside for a long time without showing it. Resentment carried in silence is heavy, especially when there's no one to tell. Because the feeling doesn't come out, no one can persuade or comfort them, and digesting anger inside yourself takes a long time. Such people, he notes, are most of all a burden to themselves and to those closest to them. This is not a reproach but a sober observation: hidden resentment goes on living. In the Rhetoric Aristotle writes that anger is appeased with time, when the offender admits fault, or when we understand there was no slight. Resentment needs a way out, not silent storage.
resentment.practice: Write a letter to the person you resent — with no intention of sending it: let the anger out, as Aristotle would advise. Notice what has changed afterward.

heartbreak.text: Aristotle asked how we should treat someone with whom closeness has ended — and answered gently: for the sake of the former warmth, keep some kindness toward them, unless a grave wrong destroyed it all. After a breakup the heart hurts almost physically, and he did not consider such pain trivial. He wrote that being in love often begins with the pleasure of seeing the beloved and can fade when that pleasure passes; but many relationships endure if the people have come to love each other's character. What was between you does not become unreal because it ended. It is part of your life, and you can remember it without hating yourself or them.
heartbreak.practice: Say aloud one thing you learned about yourself in this relationship — Aristotle would say it has already become part of your character. It stays with you.

impostor.text: Aristotle described a person who is worthy of much but thinks themselves unworthy and so allows themselves less — and called it "small-souledness," mikropsychia. The feeling that you're "not who people think you are," and that it will soon come out, visits very clever, experienced people too. Aristotle saw this not as modesty but as a mistake — false knowledge about oneself, just like vanity, only in the other direction. The measure, the "mean," here is to assess yourself as you really are. What helps is not self-confidence but sobriety: looking at what you have actually done and can do, as an impartial observer would.
impostor.practice: Picture a fair-minded outsider — the person Aristotle called practically wise — and list aloud to them three specific things you did well: facts, not impressions. What would they say?

self_hatred.text: Aristotle asked whether one can be a friend to oneself — and answered that every other friendship grows out of this one. If your inner critic sounds convincing and merciless right now, Aristotle would not agree with it. He believed the right relationship to oneself is friendship: a good person, in his words, should be a "self-lover" in the good sense — wishing themselves genuine good, caring for their mind and their life. An inner critic that hates you is not a just judge but strife within the soul. Aristotle would suggest not punishing yourself, but slowly learning to speak to yourself the way one speaks to a friend.
self_hatred.practice: Say aloud to yourself what you would say to a close friend in your situation — in the same words and the same tone. Aristotle would call this a first try at friendship with yourself.

helplessness.text: "A doctor does not deliberate whether to heal, but how," wrote Aristotle: it makes sense to deliberate only about steps within our reach. When it seems that nothing depends on you, it is one of the hardest feelings. Aristotle acknowledged that much really is beyond our control: luck, other people's decisions, circumstances. He was honest, too, that misfortunes can cloud even a good life. But he also examined in detail what he called "what is up to us" — the realm where we can deliberate and choose. Sometimes it narrows to something very small: how to respond, where to direct attention, what to ask for. Even a small choice is a real action, not a pitiful substitute for a big one. And Aristotle remembered friends: what is impossible to do alone can sometimes be done with the help of others.
helplessness.practice: Find one very small thing that depends on you right now — like the doctor who asks not "whether" but "how" — and do it. If there's someone you could ask for help, name exactly what you'd ask.

procrastination.text: "People become builders by building and lyre players by playing the lyre," wrote Aristotle. When a task just won't get started, behind it there is usually not laziness but fear, tiredness or doubt. Aristotle described a similar phenomenon when he discussed "weakness of will": a person knows what is better but acts otherwise. He distinguished two kinds: impetuosity, when we act before we've had time to think, and weakness, when we have thought but don't stick to the decision. Most important, though, is his teaching on habit: virtues are not given by nature; we become just by doing just acts. There's no need to wait for desire or confidence to appear. They come after action, not before it. You can start with something very small.
procrastination.practice: Do the first five minutes of the task you've been putting off — the way a builder lays the first stone. Promise yourself nothing more; just begin.

uprooted.text: Leaving Athens for the second time, Aristotle is said to have remarked that he would not let the Athenians sin twice against philosophy — a nod to the execution of Socrates. A native of distant Stagira, he knew well what it is to lose your footing after a move and a break with a familiar world. For Aristotle a human being is a creature that lives in community: the polis, the city, was for him the natural setting of human life. So your longing for rootedness is not a whim but a need of your nature. But Aristotle has another observation, from his books on friendship: when traveling, he writes, you can see how near and dear every human being is to every other. Roots are put down not in a place but in relationships: in friendship, shared work, recurring meetings.
uprooted.practice: Take a short walk through your new place today along a route you can repeat — the way the Peripatetics walked the paths of the Lyceum. Repetition is the first little root.

overload.text: "We work in order to have leisure, and wage war in order to live in peace," wrote Aristotle. When there are more tasks than strength, it wears you down, and it is not a weakness of yours. Aristotle valued activity, but he saw the highest good in leisure — "schole": free time for what is valuable in itself. A life made entirely of tasks is like a war without peace. Aristotle also taught the "mean": in activity, as in everything, there is excess and deficiency. An excess of tasks doesn't make life fuller — it strips it of the very thing everything is done for. Asking yourself "what am I doing this for?" is already a step toward separating the important from the superfluous.
overload.practice: List all your tasks and next to each give Aristotle's answer: "what for?" Postpone or hand off one task that has no clear answer.

unreality.text: Aristotle, a philosopher who trusted the world, considered touch the most basic of the senses: without it an animal cannot exist, and through it we come into direct contact with what is. When the world or you yourself seem distant and not quite real, as if behind glass, it is frightening, and it deserves to be described gently, without hurry. He also held that the perception of each sense's proper objects — color for sight, sound for hearing — is almost never mistaken. When thoughts about reality get tangled, the simplest sensations become your support. You don't need to settle the question of reality by reasoning. It's enough to touch something and let your body feel that it is here.
unreality.practice: Touch wood, fabric and metal in turn — the most basic of the senses, for Aristotle. Silently name three sensations: warm or cold, smooth or rough, heavy or light.

awe.text: In the Metaphysics Aristotle tells how people began to philosophize: out of wonder — first at what was close at hand, then at the movements of the Moon, the Sun and the stars overhead, at the origin of everything. The awe you feel now is that very beginning, from which all of philosophy grew. The one who wonders feels that they don't understand something and wants to understand. Your awe is not a distraction from life but a moment when what is most human in us wakes up. Aristotle considered contemplation, "theoria" (in Greek literally "looking"), the most joyful and free of activities. There's no hurry to explain your awe. You can simply linger in it and look.
awe.practice: Rest your eyes on what stirred your awe for one more minute: theoria in Greek simply means "looking." Then ask aloud one question that came up, without answering it.

quote.text: For it is owing to their wonder that men both now begin and at first began to philosophize.
quote.author: Aristotle

relief.text: Food is especially pleasant to the hungry and rest to the tired: Aristotle explained this as a return to our natural state after lack or pain. The feeling of tension finally letting go is worth noticing, without hurrying on. He wrote that such pleasures are especially vivid precisely by contrast with what came before. Your relief is a return to yourself. Body and soul seem to settle back into place. Aristotle also valued another thing: the pleasure of activity carried out without hindrance. Relief opens the way to it — to doing something again, not just holding on. You can let yourself enjoy this return.
relief.practice: Take a long exhale and notice where in your body the tension has let go — this is Aristotle's return to the natural state. Tell yourself: "That is behind me."

calm.text: Praotes — this is what Aristotle called gentleness, settling: what comes when anger has subsided, a hurt is understood, and time has done its work. He knew the worth of the calm you feel now. In the Nicomachean Ethics gentleness is a virtue, the "mean" regarding anger: the person is not indifferent, but not carried away either. And Aristotle saw the highest form of calm activity in contemplation: it is, in his words, the most continuous and self-sufficient of activities, the one in which a person needs least from outside. Your calm is neither emptiness nor laziness. It is a time when the soul is at war with nothing and can simply see. You don't have to fill it.
calm.practice: Stay in this calm for a few minutes, doing nothing — Aristotle considered contemplation the freest of activities. Just notice what you see and hear around you.

inspiration.text: Aristotle called poetry more philosophical than history: history tells what happened, poetry what could happen. Inspiration, when strength and ideas seem to arrive on their own, is a living experience of that "could." Aristotle looked at it from his own angle — through the concepts of "potentiality" and "actuality." Everything living, in his view, strives to realize what it is capable of: a seed strives to become a tree. It is the experience of your potential beginning to become actual. Aristotle wrote about poets too: in the Poetics he valued their ability to see the universal in the particular. But he was also a master of method: talent needs skill, and skill grows through practice. So inspiration is worth not only experiencing but turning into work while it's still hot.
inspiration.practice: Right now, take one small step that turns potential into actual: a sketch, a plan, a first sentence. Aristotle would say skill grows from practice, not from waiting.

schadenfreude.text: Aristotle has a long Greek word for it — epichairekakia, joy at another's misfortune; in the Ethics he places it next to envy. It's embarrassing to admit even to yourself, and yet almost everyone feels it. But he also draws a fine distinction. In the Rhetoric he writes about "indignation" — pain at undeserved success — and notes that the same person naturally feels glad when someone who acted badly is punished as they deserve. That kind of joy comes from a sense of justice, not from malice. And most importantly: Aristotle taught that we are judged not by fleeting feelings but by our settled character and our actions. A flash of schadenfreude is not a verdict on you. It's just useful to ask where it comes from: hurt, envy or a sense of justice.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself Aristotle's question and answer aloud in one word: what am I glad about — justice, relief, or that someone is worse off? An honest word already weakens the feeling's hold.

contempt.text: Aristotle noticed that contempt is the flip side of emulation: whoever greatly values intelligence, courage or honesty tends to look down on those who lack them. It is a cold feeling, awkward to admit, but it can tell a lot about you. In the Rhetoric Aristotle examined it as one kind of "slight": to feel contempt is to regard someone or something as worth nothing. Your contempt may point to what truly matters to you. But Aristotle also knew the cost of this feeling: a slight, by his observation, is the main cause of other people's anger. There's no need to shame yourself for contempt. It's more useful to ask what value it is protecting, and whether you can serve that value without belittling another person.
contempt.practice: Say aloud to yourself: "I look down on this because what matters to me is…" — and today do one small thing in which that value shows up in you yourself.

disgust.text: Heraclitus, warming himself at a kitchen stove, told his hesitant visitors, "Come in, there are gods here too" — Aristotle tells the story in On the Parts of Animals. Disgust is a strong, almost bodily reaction, and you can't simply "switch it off." Aristotle admits that studying some creatures and their inner workings is unpleasant, but urges us not to turn away childishly: in every natural thing there is something worth marveling at. Disgust, then, is a first reaction, not the last word. Sometimes behind it lies protection from something truly harmful, sometimes just unfamiliarity. Disgust with yourself can be examined just as calmly: it is a feeling, not the truth about your worth.
disgust.practice: Look at what disgusts you (or recall it) through the eyes of Aristotle the naturalist: what exactly — a sight, a smell, an action, a thought? Name the reaction separately from the object — that already helps.

revenge.text: Aristotle honestly admitted what moralists prefer to keep quiet: anticipating a counterblow is pleasant. The wish for revenge is usually born of real pain, and it has its own logic. In the Rhetoric Aristotle defined anger as pain and a desire to answer a slight. He didn't consider the feeling monstrous. But in the Nicomachean Ethics he also described gentleness: a mild person is not vengeful but rather inclined to forgive, though they don't let themselves be trampled. And in his teaching on justice he showed another path: a broken equality should be restored by a third, impartial party — a judge, a mediator — not by the injured person themselves. The wish for revenge is a signal: there was an injustice. You can hear it without turning it into action, and seek restoration rather than a counterblow.
revenge.practice: Picture the impartial judge Aristotle wrote about and tell them aloud: "I was treated unjustly because…" Then ask: what would restore equality without harming anyone?

anger_at_loved.text: "We are angrier with friends than with strangers," Aristotle notes in the Rhetoric: from them we expect good. Anger at a partner, parents, children can be especially sharp, and then shame follows. In the Politics he notes the same thing: spirit rises most strongly against those close to us when we feel they have slighted us. This is no sign that there's no love — on the contrary, the anger here grows out of expectations that exist only in closeness. The measure, the "mean," matters most of all with those you love. You can acknowledge your feeling and express it without wounding: with words, with a pause, with a conversation once the wave has subsided.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, step out for a few minutes and walk like a Peripatetic. As you go, name to yourself which expectation was broken — that's where a calm conversation can begin.

ambivalence.text: Aristotle described the bond between parents and children as a friendship of unequals — with disputes, reproaches, and love all the same. Loving someone close and not being able to stand them at once is confusing and sometimes frightening, but he would see nothing unnatural in it. He wrote that the soul has different parts — rational and non-rational — and they can pull in different directions. In the Rhetoric he showed that many feelings are mixed by their very nature: anger contains both pain and pleasure, and we get angriest precisely with those we love. Your mixed feelings are not a mistake but a sign of a complex, living bond. They don't need to be reduced to one.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a page into two columns: "what I love in this person" and "what I find hard to bear." Let both be true at once — as in Aristotle's friendship of unequals.

guilty_relief.text: Aristotle distinguished feelings from judgments about oneself: we don't choose to be frightened or glad, only how to act. Relief you feel ashamed of — after a breakup, a departure, even the death of someone close who had long been ill — is one of the quietest and heaviest feelings, and it does not contradict love. He wrote about mixed states in which pain and pleasure combine, and about pleasure as a return to the natural state after long strain. If you carried a weight for a long time — of caregiving, fear, uncertainty — then relief that it has been lifted is natural. It doesn't cancel your love and grief; it exists alongside them. Relief speaks of how long things were hard for you, not of any coldness in you.
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself: "I feel lighter, and I loved." Then write down what weight you carried all this time — that is the answer to where the relief comes from.

indifference.text: A truly insensible person, Aristotle observed, is a great rarity: such insensibility "is not human," for feeling belongs to our nature. So when something "should" move you and inside it is quiet, it is frightening — but most likely it is a temporary state, not who you are. But another of his observations matters more: feelings, he wrote, arise in us without choice — we don't decide to be frightened or angry. So demanding the "right" feeling from yourself on command makes no sense. Indifference may be a sign of tiredness, overload or protection, when the soul has had too much. For Aristotle, we are responsible for our actions, not for momentary feelings. You can act with care even if your heart is quiet for now, and give the feeling time.
indifference.practice: Instead of "why don't I feel anything?" ask: "How tired have I been lately?" — and today do one caring act for yourself or someone else without waiting for the feeling. For Aristotle, the act can come first.

escape.text: After Plato's death Aristotle left Athens for the island of Lesbos, where for years he studied fish, cuttlefish and sea urchins in a lagoon — the move became a new science. The wish to drop everything and leave — a job, a city, a role — is strongest when life has grown cramped. Aristotle helps us take this wish seriously, but without haste. He taught us to "take counsel with ourselves" — to deliberate not about the goal but about the ways to it: what exactly do I want to change, and by what means? He also described courage as a mean between cowardice and rashness: there is courage in staying and courage in leaving. The wish to run away is a signal that you are missing something important: leisure, freedom, meaning. It's worth hearing it out and asking what exactly you are looking for.
escape.practice: Finish the sentence: "If I left, I could finally…" For Aristotle, that is the goal, and moving is only one of the paths to it. Could you give yourself at least part of it right now?

forbidden_attraction.text: Aristotle distinguished what happens to us from what we choose: we are not praised or blamed for being frightened or angry — only for our actions. Being drawn to someone "off-limits," unavailable or "wrong," is confusing and brings shame, but he would not judge the feeling itself. In his books on friendship he noted that love often begins with the pleasure of seeing the other person, and goodwill with seeing something good in them. Attraction may be telling you about what draws you: liveliness, attention, freedom, something missing from your life. Decisions about actions are a separate question, and for those Aristotle valued practical wisdom and time.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Imagine this attraction is a letter from your own life. Which quality in it is asking for attention — liveliness, being noticed, freedom? Name it aloud and think about where else it might be found.

social_anxiety.text: "Shame dwells in the eyes" — Aristotle quotes this old proverb to explain why we find it hardest under other people's gaze. Fear of people and their judgment is agonizing, and you are far from alone in it. In the Rhetoric Aristotle described shame as pain and disturbance about things that may harm our reputation, and noted that we feel it above all before those whose opinion we value. In the Nicomachean Ethics he speaks of a "mean" in this feeling: there is the shameless person who doesn't care, and the bashful one who, as he puts it, is ashamed of everything. The good lies somewhere in between. Your shyness is the extreme of a feeling that is natural and even valuable in itself. Aristotle would add that shame is fitting for our actions, not for simply being who we are and looking the way we look.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a get-together, take three calm breaths out and silently name the two or three people whose opinion here really matters to you. You can let the other gazes go — shame belongs only before those we value.

uncertainty.text: "Will there be a sea battle tomorrow?" Aristotle examines this question in On Interpretation, and logicians still argue over his answer. Wanting to know what will happen when knowing is impossible is hard — and Aristotle took it very seriously. Today the statement "there will be" is not yet definitely true or false — the future really is open. This is not a flaw in our knowledge but a property of the future itself. And in the Nicomachean Ethics he advises not demanding more precision from a subject than it allows: in matters of life we judge "in outline" and "for the most part." Your uncertainty is honest: you see the world as it is. The question is not how to know the future, but what it is reasonable to do now.
uncertainty.practice: Name aloud three ways things might turn out — as Aristotle would weigh the outcomes of the sea battle — and for each, one thing you would do. The future stays open, but you have a plan.

waiting.text: Aristotle defined time as "the number of motion": we notice it when something changes. Waiting — for results, an answer, news — wears you out because almost nothing depends on you right now, and time seems to have frozen. Aristotle distinguished "potentiality" and "actuality": what may happen and what has already happened. Waiting is life between the two, when the outcome is not yet settled. In On Interpretation he showed that the future really is open until it arrives. Waiting likely drags on so long because attention has frozen on one point and nothing is moving. Aristotle would suggest putting motion back into time: turn to what depends on you while the rest is being decided.
waiting.practice: Set a time when you'll next check the news or your email, and until then put motion back into time: take up one small task you can finish.

regret.text: The finest tragic hero, for Aristotle, is Oedipus: he is ruined not by wickedness but by an error, hamartia, made in ignorance. Regret over something done or left undone can be very bitter, and Aristotle considered it an important feeling. He wrote that a weak-willed person, unlike a vicious one, regrets their actions — and that is precisely why they can change: the right values are alive in them. And if we acted out of ignorance and grieve over it later, Aristotle did not consider such an act truly voluntary: you didn't know then what you know now. Regret is not proof that you're a bad person but a sign that you've grown and see more clearly. Aristotle taught that character is formed by repeated actions. The past can't be changed, but it can become a lesson for your next choice.
regret.practice: Write: "Back then I didn't know…" and "Now I know…" Then one thing you'll do differently in a similar situation: that, for Aristotle, is how character grows out of error.

longing.text: Friends, Aristotle wrote, want above all to live together: to talk, share everyday life, do things side by side. So when you miss one particular person, what hurts is not abstract loneliness but the absence of exactly them. A friend, in his words, is "another self," and in their presence we feel our own life more fully. Hence the pain of separation. But Aristotle offers a comforting distinction: distance, he writes, interrupts not the friendship as such but only its activity — the life lived together. The attachment itself, the settled disposition of the soul, remains. Your longing is a form of that bond. It says that this person is still part of your life, even if they aren't near.
longing.practice: Tell this person — or, if they can't be reached, someone else — about one specific thing you loved doing together. For Aristotle, this briefly renews the activity of friendship.

world_pain.text: In the theater of Dionysus thousands of Athenians wept together over others' misfortunes — Aristotle called it "catharsis," a purification through pity and fear. Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — can be almost unbearable. In the Rhetoric Aristotle examined two related feelings. Pity: pain at the sight of undeserved misfortune that could also happen to us. Indignation: pain at the sight of undeserved success. He considered both signs of a good character. And in the Poetics he showed that pain lived through together with others becomes something that can be borne. Your pain is a sign that you are not indifferent to human fate. But Aristotle also taught measure: so as not to burn out, you need to share this weight with others and find within it a task that is within your strength.
world_pain.practice: Today, limit the news to one set time and give the freed minutes to one thing within your strength — help, a conversation, a kind word to someone nearby. That, for Aristotle, is how compassion finds its measure.

rejection.text: Honor, Aristotle noticed, depends more on those who give it than on the one who receives it — which is why it is too shallow to be the measure of a person. Being rejected wounds painfully, and he understood why. In the Rhetoric he writes that what stings us most is a "slight" — when we, our words or our qualities are not taken seriously. It is one of the main causes of anger and sadness. Aristotle also soberly wrote that many bonds are built for pleasure or usefulness and fall apart when circumstances change — through no one's fault. A refusal speaks about circumstances and another person's choice; it does not pass a verdict on you.
rejection.practice: List aloud three qualities you value in yourself regardless of this rejection — the part of you that, for Aristotle, does not depend on anyone's recognition.

abandonment.text: "People cannot know each other until they have eaten the proverbial salt together," Aristotle quotes an old saying. The fear of being abandoned can live very deep and unsettle you more than anything. Aristotle considered attachment to people part of human nature, so the need itself is natural. He also wrote about how lasting closeness is built: trust takes time and a shared life. The fear likely grows when your support is too narrow: when your whole life rests on one person. Aristotle valued "self-sufficiency" — not solitude, but a life with several supports: friends, work, treating yourself as a friend. The more of them there are, the less the fear of one loss governs everything.
abandonment.practice: Name three supports in your life besides the person you're afraid of losing, and give one of them a little time today — a call, a meeting, a favorite activity. That, for Aristotle, is how trust grows.

unrequited.text: Aristotle gives the example of mothers who delight in loving their child even when the child cannot respond: loving, in his view, matters more than being loved, and there is a strength of the lover's own in this. Love left unanswered wounds painfully, and he took that pain seriously, calling it neither foolish nor weak. In the Nicomachean Ethics he writes that the lover often complains that his excessive love goes unanswered. Your feeling is not a useless mistake. The capacity to love is your own strength, and it stays with you. But Aristotle valued reciprocity too: love is fullest in equality, and you deserve a feeling that answers yours.
unrequited.practice: Do something warm today for someone who can respond — a friend or a family member. Aristotle valued reciprocity: let your capacity to love work where it will be answered.

humiliation.text: Hubris, insolence — this is what Aristotle called shaming another for the pleasure of feeling superior. When you've been humiliated, it feels as if your very worth has been struck, and it is one of the most painful experiences. He saw this as the wrongdoing of the one who humiliates, not of the one humiliated. In the Nicomachean Ethics he added that it is fitting to be ashamed of our own bad actions — what depends on us — not of what was done to us. The shame you feel rightly belongs not to you. Aristotle considered anger at humiliation an entirely natural response. Your dignity has not vanished because someone tried to take it away.
humiliation.practice: Tell yourself: "This was done to me, but it doesn't make me less." Write down what was hurt and what in you remained untouched: for Aristotle, the wrongdoing here belongs to someone else.

body_shame.text: For Aristotle the soul is not a passenger in a shell but the "form" of a living body: if the eye were a living creature, sight would be its soul. Dissatisfaction with your body can be quiet and constant, and that doesn't make it easier. Aristotle saw the body differently from many who came after him. The body is not a picture to be graded but that through which we see, hear, touch, act and rejoice. He acknowledged that external goods, beauty included, matter for a life, but happiness, in his view, is above all activity: what we do, understand and experience. Your body matters not for how it looks to others but for the fact that it lets you live. You might try treating it as a companion.
body_shame.practice: Name three things your body let you do today — walk, hug, taste something. Aristotle would say that is where the soul lives, not in a reflection.

illness.text: A good general, Aristotle wrote, makes the best use of the army he has, and a shoemaker makes the finest shoe from the leather he is given. Illness, when the body lets you down, is draining and frightening, and he didn't pretend it was a trifle. He honestly admitted that a happy life needs external goods too, and that heavy misfortunes can cloud even a good life. But he also wrote that happiness is not so easily taken away: it lies in the activity of the soul, which is possible even in constrained circumstances. And through hardship, he observed, nobility shines when a person bears it with dignity. Illness narrows the field, but it does not cancel your life.
illness.practice: Find one small thing within your reach today despite the illness — a conversation, reading, a minute by the window — and do it wholeheartedly, as Aristotle's craftsman works with what he has.

pride.text: Aristotle considered false modesty as much a mistake as boasting, and called "greatness of soul" the ability of someone worthy of much to know it calmly. Pride in what you've done is a good, healthy feeling, and he didn't urge us to hide it: there is nothing shameful in it. The Nicomachean Ethics has a lovely observation about makers: a craftsman loves his work more than the work could love him, as poets love their poems like children. The reason is that in what they make, a person in a sense realizes themselves: their activity becomes visible. Your pride is joy that your potential has become actual. You can enjoy it openly.
pride.practice: Say aloud: "I did this" — and list the qualities it took. Aristotle would call this honest self-knowledge, not boasting.

melancholy.text: "Why is it that all who have become eminent in philosophy, politics, poetry or the arts are melancholics?" asks the Problems, a collection from Aristotle's school. A bright sadness, where sorrow mingles with depth and even beauty, is a subtle state, and this school treated it with respect. The authorship of this text is disputed, but the idea itself became famous: melancholy is linked to depth and the capacity to see. And in the Poetics Aristotle wrote of the particular pleasure tragedy gives, and of "catharsis" — purification through pity and fear. Your melancholy may be not a malfunction but a way of feeling the world more deeply. You don't have to drive it away; you can spend some time with it.
melancholy.practice: Listen to music or reread poems in tune with your mood — Aristotle wrote of the particular pleasure tragedy gives. Notice what is beautiful in this sadness.
